第 8 章 Communicating with Executives与高管沟通

Travis Kimmel / 特拉维斯·金梅尔

— 第 34 页 —

Early in my career as an engineering manager, I would become frustrated when upper management seemingly brushed off challenges in engineering or asked me questions that seemed irrelevant. My perception was that the non-technical side of the business was out of touch or even at odds against technical initiatives—to the detriment of the business as I saw it.

刚做工程经理时，我经常很沮丧——高层好像对工程方面的挑战不屑一顾，或者问一些看起来毫不相干的问题。我当时觉得业务的非技术层面完全脱离现实，甚至和技术举措对着干——在我看来这损害了公司利益。

In hindsight this all makes a bit more sense. As organizations grow, an inevitable amount of complexity is introduced. The sheer variety of projects, people, and responsibilities on the minds of those at the top can be overwhelming.

事后看来，这一切就说得通了。随着组织成长，不可避免地会引入复杂度。高层脑子里要装的项目、人员、责任种类之多，可能是压倒性的。

In my tenure as CEO, I've learned how to navigate a constant stream of demands competing for my attention, where it is not possible to unpack complex topics in real time. I now recognize the problem was probably two-fold. First, senior leaders faced raw, demanding items and were often fighting fires where mine wasn't the priority. Second, I probably didn't communicate in a way that got their attention.

在我担任 CEO 期间，我学会了如何应对不断涌来、争夺我注意力的各种需求——在这种情况下，不可能实时把复杂话题讲透。我现在认识到问题可能有两方面。第一，高层面对的是各种原始的、急迫的事务，经常在灭火，而我的事不是优先级最高的。第二，我大概没有用能引起他们注意的方式来沟通。

Here are a few tips for communicating with and presenting to executives that have held true for me in the years since joining the ranks of management:

以下是我做管理这些年总结的、和高管沟通汇报的几个技巧：

The granularity of your conversations should scale to match your company size对话的粒度应随公司规模调整

On the smallest teams, you might spend time talking about specific tasks. A bit larger, and you're talking about sprints or collections of tasks. At hundreds or thousands of employees, you're likely talking in terms of broad themes of work or long-term initiatives and resource allocation.

在最小的团队里，你可能讨论具体任务。大一点，你讨论的是 Sprint 或任务集合。到了几百上千人的公司，你大概就在讨论宽泛的工作主题或长期计划和资源分配了。

As the company scales, you'll be expected to be more independent when it comes to managing tactical concerns, and focusing your communication on larger themes as the company grows (while continuing to handle lower-level items autonomously) is an important signal that you as a leader are scaling with the company.

随着公司扩张，你应该在战术层面的事务上更加独立，并且在公司成长时把沟通重点放在更大的主题上（同时继续自主处理低层事务）——这是你作为领导者在和公司一起成长的重要信号。

— 第 35 页 —

Push information up frequently without being asked to do so主动频繁向上推送信息，不等要求

Depending on your role, you might not be speaking directly to senior leadership on a regular basis. Your manager might be, however, so it's helpful to consider them as a communication channel. Keep your manager in the loop proactively even when things are going well. It's easy to slip into firefighting mode, but pushing bursty updates about things being on track is often just as valuable, and it gives you an opportunity to showcase the work your team is doing.

根据你的角色，你可能不直接和高层定期对话。但你的经理可能会，所以把他们当作沟通渠道是有帮助的。即使一切顺利，也要主动让经理知情。人很容易掉进「只在救火时才沟通」的模式，但推送简短的「一切正常」更新往往同样有价值，而且给你展示团队工作的机会。

The patterns for communicating upward are almost the inverse of communication with your team向上沟通的模式几乎和向下沟通相反

Team-centric communication is often about fostering autonomy, and overcommunication at that layer can be distracting or come off as condescending. Upward communication is the opposite: rarely will you run into a problem overcommunicating, and the larger the company, the more bursty updates serve as valuable reminders to your stakeholders about everything currently in play.

对团队的沟通通常是为了培养自主权，那个层面过度沟通可能让人分心或显得居高临下。向上沟通恰恰相反：你几乎不会因为过度沟通而出问题。公司越大，简短的更新就越能作为有价值的提醒，让利益相关方知道当前有哪些事在进行中。

Tell them what you're going to tell them, tell them, and then tell them what you told them先说你要讲什么，再讲，然后总结你讲了什么

It's a natural tendency to want to build the story before finally landing on the thesis. That might work for a TED talk, but it doesn't really work in an executive setting. Tell them what you're going to tell them. "We'd like to spend three weeks paying down technical debt. Today I'm going to discuss why we'd like to do that and what we're focusing on, and I would like to leave with a 'go' or a 'no-go' decision." Do that and then provide a summary of what you told them (ideally in written form) and restate the goals of your communication with a concrete ask or information about when the next update will happen.

人很自然地想先铺垫故事再得出结论。这在 TED 演讲里可能行得通，但在高管场景里不行。先告诉他们你要讲什么。「我们想花三周时间偿还技术债。今天我会讨论为什么要这么做、重点是什么，我希望离开时得到一个做还是不做的决定。」然后做总结（最好以书面形式），重申沟通目标，并给出一个具体的请求或下次更新的时间。

Think of it as a three-step process that does the following:

把它想成三步：

  1. I'm telling you about X because of Y.我跟你说 X 是因为 Y。
  2. Here are the details on X.以下是 X 的细节。
  3. I need you to do Z so that I can accomplish X because of Y.我需要你做 Z，这样我才能因为 Y 完成 X。

This pattern is very effective with executives; it helps frontload your message with information about why the conversation is important as well as what you need in terms of executive backing and mandate:

这个模式对高管非常有效；它帮你把「为什么这次谈话重要」以及「你需要高管提供什么支持和授权」的信息前置：

— 第 36 页 —

Write the narrative first先写叙事稿

Before you begin thinking about the presentation, write a narrative explaining your argument and recommendation. Organize your thoughts in writing first as if your manager were going to review it. This will help identify gaps in your understanding of the problem and give you a template for following up in writing after the conversation. Done well, it will help you sufficiently consider and address the various perspectives and constraints of the problem—and after you've prepped at this level you will rarely be caught out when you're advocating to a larger audience.

在开始想演示之前，先写一份叙事稿，解释你的论点和建议。先以书面形式整理思路，就像你的经理要审阅它一样。这会帮你发现对问题理解的盲点，也为会后书面跟进提供模板。做得好的话，它会帮你充分考虑和应对问题的各种视角和约束——做到这个准备程度后，在更大的受众面前陈述时你几乎不会被问倒。

Creating a presentation is much easier after the narrative is written. I like to write out the narrative, trim the fat, and build slides around it.

叙事稿写完后，做演示就容易多了。我喜欢先写好叙事稿，删繁就简，然后围绕它做幻灯片。

Don't be evasive, and prepare for detours别回避问题，准备好被岔开

Senior leaders will frequently pierce into areas that they see as potential problems, sometimes uncovering gaps in the presenter's understanding of the problem. These unexpected questions can quickly derail the entire presentation toward a thread of follow-up questions as they dig even further. Presentations to executives that take an unexpected turn are common; their experience has helped tune their radar for knowing when to dive in further.

高层经常会深入他们认为有问题的领域，有时会暴露汇报者对问题理解的盲区。这些意外问题可能很快让整个汇报偏离轨道，变成一连串追问。给高管做汇报时出现意外转折很常见；他们的经验让他们的雷达很准，知道什么时候该深挖。

Along the same vein, answer their questions directly. Executive radar quickly picks up on evasive answers, so err on the side of "I don't know but I'll find out" as opposed to vamping. It's generally fine not to know something, and if you take detailed notes and follow up after this will almost always work to your advantage.

同样，直接回答他们的问题。高管的雷达很快就能察觉到回避式回答，所以宁可说「我不知道，但我会去查」也不要胡编。不知道某些事通常没关系，如果你认真记笔记、事后跟进，这几乎总是对你有利的。

Numbers are the language of business数字是商业的语言

Use data to explain the current constraints, context, or progress of the problem. If you don't provide data and instead skip to the analysis, you're relying on trust and persuasion to get the information, guidance, or resources that you need. Executives are by nature very results oriented, so make sure anything you propose is coupled with data that will allow them to process the problem themselves in a "show your work" fashion.

用数据解释问题当前的约束、背景或进展。如果你不提供数据而是直接跳到分析，那你就在靠信任和说服力来获取你需要的信息、指导或资源。高管天生非常结果导向，所以确保你提出的任何建议都附带数据，让他们能以「展示你的推导过程」的方式自己处理问题。

The ideal outcome of a meeting is one where everyone leaves with shared understanding of the path ahead, and the surest way to get there is inclusion of the data that led you to your own conclusions.

会议的理想结果是每个人离开时对未来方向有共识，而达到这个目标最可靠的方式就是把引导你得出结论的数据包含进来。

— 第 37 页 —

Lead with the ask先提请求

Go into the meeting with a clear goal. Start the meeting by explicitly framing the goal, and then return to the ask at the end of the meeting. Executive time is precious, so make sure to be respectful of that by having a clear outcome for the meeting. It's generally better to be a little over-ambitious in your ask than it is to meander about without obvious action items.

带着明确目标进会议。开场就明确说明目标，结尾再回到请求上。高管的时间很宝贵，所以要尊重这一点——会议要有明确的产出。一般来说，请求稍微大一点总比漫无目的、没有明确行动项好。
